summary:
Niger is among the most dangerous countries in the region for a trans visitor. Same-sex conduct was outlawed explicitly for the first time in March 2025, when Article 25 of the ruling junta's Charter of Refoundation banned “LGBTQIA+ practices or any other unnatural behavior” during the five-year transition declared after the July 2023 coup. That article set no specific penalties; a February 2026 revision of the penal code supplied them.

Article 390 of the 2026 code criminalises “indecent, unnatural, and LGBTQIA+ acts” with five to ten years' imprisonment and fines of up to 100 million CFA francs. Article 391 punishes same-sex marriage with ten to twenty years. Article 392 targets LGBTQIA+ associations. The code also reaches anyone who “artificially changes sex at birth” or attempts to, and covers public announcement of a same-sex relationship. Mitigating circumstances and suspended sentences are unavailable under these provisions.

Enforcement since the code took effect has been wide. At least 40 people have been arrested for homosexuality and 16 men, including high-ranking military officials, imprisoned. Campaigners describe a witch-hunt in a toxic climate, local media reported dozens of arrests across the country, and LGBTQ people have gone into hiding.

Organisation offences are punished with ten to twenty years' imprisonment and fines of up to 500 million CFA francs (about US$882,829) for creating, managing, financing or participating, directly or indirectly, in LGBTQIA+ organisations, clubs and social venues.

Access to HIV prevention has collapsed. Organisations providing services to men who have sex with men stopped working after the 2026 law, and a representative warned that people no longer have access to condoms, HIV testing or PrEP; campaigners fear an HIV/AIDS resurgence.

The justice minister has said that “all LGBTQ practices, whatever they may be” are “not in line with our social and cultural values”. Niger has no broad legal protections against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.
tangentialFactors:
Niger's 2026 legislation sits within a wider pattern of African states hardening anti-LGBTQIA+ laws, and its drafting is broad enough that commentators read asexuality as sanctionable conduct. Human rights scholars describe the code as violating the rights of intersex as well as LGBTQIA+ people.

Criminalisation did not arrive in a single step. In December 2022 lawmakers backed a motion to criminalise same-sex relationships, moved by an MP from the southern Maradi region, weeks after a Maradi court acquitted two young women of lesbianism charges precisely because no legislation criminalised same-sex relationships. A 2023 draft penal code proposed up to five years for same-sex conduct, twenty years for conducting, officiating or witnessing a same-sex marriage, and five years for participating in or financing “homosexual” organisations.

Under the pre-2025 rules the age of consent was unequal: thirteen for different-sex acts against twenty-one for same-sex acts.

A 2013 United States State Department human rights report found no reports of violence based on sexual orientation or gender identity and no documented cases of discrimination, while cautioning that stigma or intimidation probably kept incidents unreported; the same report recorded two men caught naked in a parked car arrested for public indecency and fined. Those findings predate the current criminalisation regime.

Societal stigma is documented. Asylum seekers from Cameroon, Liberia and Côte d'Ivoire who staged Niger's first LGBTQ public demonstration in Niamey in 2022 faced discrimination including shops refusing to serve them and verbal or physical violence from strangers, and Niger's authorities refused to recognise their refugee status.
localsOnly:
Residents have been prosecuted under public-indecency provisions for years. In Maradi in 2022 two young women were prosecuted over alleged lesbianism and acquitted because no legislation then existed, but were imprisoned for two years for posting nude videos on social media allegedly portraying a lesbian act. In 2023 two women were prosecuted for alleged same-sex intimacy under public-indecency Article 276, which carries up to three years, and the trial judge was reassigned to an administrative post after acquitting them. In Niamey in 2025 two young women reported by a third person were prosecuted for public indecency and acquitted because the facts did not pertain to the public sphere; the judge was allegedly sanctioned for being too lenient.

Two gay rights organisations reportedly operated in secret in Niger, partly because they were not formally registered. After the 2026 penal code, organisations providing HIV prevention services to men who have sex with men stopped working.

Niger's only statutory protections touching sexual orientation were narrow. Article 95 of Law 2022-59 on the Protection of Personal Data prohibits collecting or processing data revealing sexual orientation, punishable by three months to five years' imprisonment and fines of 5,000,000 to 50,000,000 CFA francs; the law was published by the Ministry of Communication and New Information Technologies in June 2025. The only other protection, in Article 4 of Law 2015-36 on Illicit Trafficking of Migrants, was repealed in 2023 by decree of President Abdourahamane Tiani, with prior convictions and their effects expunged.

Historically many LGBTQ Nigeriens led socially acceptable public lives while keeping relationships private; since the 2026 law they have gone into hiding. Stigmatisation among the broader population is widespread. Public discourse was shaped in 2023 by proposals from President Mohamed Bazoum that framed the issue as “social contagion”.
outOfScopeNotes:
No sourced entry, visa, or passport and gender-marker rules for visitors to Niger appear in the inventory; those questions remain unresolved rather than answered negatively.

The penalty for organisation offences is reported inconsistently across sources: a 2023 draft code proposed five years, while the account of the February 2026 code gives ten to twenty years with fines up to 500 million CFA francs. The official consolidated text of the 2026 penal code has not been consulted here.

Arrest and imprisonment totals since the 2026 law rest on campaigner and press reporting and have not been independently verified.

The United States State Department human rights report cited for the absence of documented violence dates from 2013 and predates both the 2025 charter and the 2026 code.
